lead: Every liquid extractor does two jobs: mix the feed with solvent to make interfacial area, then let the two liquids settle into layers. A mixer-settler does them in two vessels; a column does them in one tall vessel. The mixer volume sets contact time, the settler area sets separation, and a column's height sets the number of transfer units. These ideas size equipment from a beaker test to a plant treating hundreds of cubic metres per hour, as in recovery of acetic acid or purification of antibiotics.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for phase splitting, 5.3 for stage counts, Unit 2 for stage efficiency, and Unit 3 for HTU, NTU and flooding.

blocks.text: In a mixer-settler, feed and solvent enter a stirred mixer. The stirrer breaks one phase into drops. The drops give interfacial area for solute transfer. The mixture then flows to a settler, a wide shallow tank. Gravity makes drops rise or fall and coalesce. Two layers leave: extract (solvent-rich) and raffinate (carrier-rich).
The mixer is sized by residence time. A long time gives more transfer but a larger vessel. The settler is sized by the area needed for drops to settle, not by the total flow.

blocks.where: t is the mean residence time in the mixer (h); V is the mixer volume (m³); Q is the total combined feed plus solvent flow (m³/h).
A is the settler horizontal area (m²); Q<sub>d</sub> is the dispersed-phase volumetric flow (m³/h); v<sub>s</sub> is the settling velocity of the drops (m/h).

blocks.text: Stage efficiency E is the fraction of the equilibrium change actually achieved in one real stage. If a stage reaches 80% of equilibrium, E = 0.8. The number of real units is N<sub>real</sub> = N<sub>theoretical</sub> / E. This is not the same as N<sub>theoretical</sub>.

A column contacts two liquids counter-currently in one vessel. One phase is dispersed as drops; the other is continuous. The dispersed phase should be the one that wets the packing less, so it forms drops instead of coating the surface. In a spray column, nozzles make drops and there is no packing. In a packed column, packing breaks drops and reduces axial mixing, but it can also trap drops and reduce capacity.

Key variables are drop size d, dispersed-phase hold-up φ (volume of drops per volume of column), and flooding. Smaller drops give more area a but settle slowly, so hold-up rises and the column floods at lower flow. Axial mixing, or back mixing, reduces the concentration driving force.

blocks.where: Z is the packed height (m); H<sub>oc</sub> is the overall height of a transfer unit (m); N<sub>oc</sub> is the number of overall transfer units (dimensionless). H<sub>oc</sub> falls as interfacial area per volume and overall mass transfer coefficient rise.

blocks.text: Mechanically agitated contactors add stirrers or plates. A rotating-disc contactor (RDC) uses spinning discs on a shaft; a reciprocating-plate column (RPC) moves perforated plates up and down. Both give smaller drops and higher hold-up, so they need less height. Pulsed units are in 5.6.

A mixer-settler gives one equilibrium stage per mixer plus settler. Columns give many stages in one shell. For a small number of stages and dirty liquids, a mixer-settler is easy to clean. For many stages and clean liquids, a column saves floor space and solvent inventory.

Capacity means throughput per unit area or volume. Stages per unit height matters when the building is tall. Floor space matters in revamps. Solvent inventory matters for safety and cost, because solvent is often flammable or expensive.

figure.caption: Feed and solvent enter the mixer where drops form; the settler then separates the two layers into extract and raffinate. Notice that mixing and settling are separate vessels.

spec.title: One mixer-settler stage
spec.aria: Feed and solvent join in the mixer, the mixed stream goes to the settler, and the settler sends out two separate streams, the extract and the raffinate.

examples.question: A mixer-settler stage handles 2 m³/h of combined feed and solvent. The mixer holds 0.5 m³. The dispersed phase flow is 1 m³/h and its drops settle at 0.6 m/h. Find the mixing time in hours and minutes, and the settler area required.
steps: Data: combined flow Q = 2 m³/h; mixer volume V = 0.5 m³; dispersed-phase flow Q<sub>d</sub> = 1 m³/h; settling velocity v<sub>s</sub> = 0.6 m/h.
Mixing time: t = V / Q = 0.5 m³ ÷ 2 m³/h = 0.25 h.
Convert to minutes: 0.25 h × 60 min/h = 15 min.
Settler area: A = Q<sub>d</sub> / v<sub>s</sub> = 1 m³/h ÷ 0.6 m/h = 1.6667 m².
Unit check: (m³/h) ÷ (m/h) = m², so the area unit is correct.
examples.answer: Mixing time is 0.25 h (15 min); settler area is 1.6667 m².
examples.check:
Q = 2.0
V = 0.5
Qd = 1.0
vs = 0.6
t = V / Q
tm = t * 60
A = Qd / vs
print(round(t, 4))
print(round(tm, 4))
print(round(A, 4))

traps: Sizing the settler on the total flow instead of the dispersed-phase flow. Only Q<sub>d</sub> settles; the continuous phase leaves as a separate layer.
Quoting stage efficiency as if it were the number of stages. E is a fraction per stage; N<sub>real</sub> = N<sub>theoretical</sub> / E.
Forgetting which phase is dispersed. Changing the dispersed phase changes Q<sub>d</sub>, drop size and settling velocity.
Using mixer volume to size the settler, or settler area to find contact time. The mixer sets time; the settler sets separation area.
Treating flooding as one fixed velocity for all columns. Flooding depends on drop size, hold-up, packing and flow ratio.

quiz.q: What two jobs must every extraction equipment do?
quiz.a: Mix the two liquids to create interfacial area, and let the two liquids settle into separate layers.

quiz.q: Why is a settler sized on dispersed-phase flow, not total flow?
quiz.a: Only the dispersed drops must rise or fall through the continuous phase. The continuous phase does not settle through itself, so total flow would overestimate the area.

quiz.q: A mixer holds 0.8 m³ and combined flow is 4 m³/h. Find the mixing time in hours and minutes.
quiz.a: t = V/Q = 0.8/4 = 0.2 h. In minutes, 0.2 × 60 = 12 min.

quiz.q: Dispersed-phase flow is 0.5 m³/h and settling velocity is 0.25 m/h. Find the settler area.
Why should the phase that wets packing less be the dispersed phase?
quiz.a: If it wets the packing, it coats the surface and forms a film instead of drops. Drops give interfacial area; a film gives little area and can block the column.

quiz.q: A packed extraction column floods when the flow is raised. Give two changes that could raise capacity and one trade-off for each.
quiz.a: Use larger drops or less packing to reduce hold-up and raise capacity, but area falls so height rises. Reduce dispersed-phase flow, but throughput falls. Change the dispersed phase, but settling and mass transfer change.

quiz.q: Compare a mixer-settler battery and a mechanically agitated column for 8 stages and 50 m³/h of clean liquids.
quiz.a: A mixer-settler battery needs 8 mixers and 8 settlers, so floor space and solvent inventory are large, but each stage is easy to inspect. A mechanically agitated column gives many stages in one small shell, so floor space and solvent inventory are lower, but maintenance and scale-up are harder.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern plants use computational fluid dynamics to predict drop size and hold-up before building a column. Membrane contactors keep the phases separate at a porous wall, so they avoid flooding but add membrane resistance. Miniature mixer-settlers are used for continuous production of fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Search for RDC extraction column, axial mixing in extraction columns and CFD-PBM extraction if you want the research view.
